html:
The Great Mosque of Córdoba was begun in 785 by Abd al-Rahman I, the first Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus, and enlarged over two centuries. Since 1236 it has been a cathedral.

Its hall is a forest of more than 800 columns of marble and stone, carrying double arches striped in red brick and white stone. The prayer niche, added in the 960s under the Caliphate of Córdoba, is covered in gold mosaics made with Byzantine help. Córdoba was then one of the largest and richest cities in Europe.

When Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba during the Reconquista, the mosque was consecrated as a church. In the 1500s a Renaissance cathedral was built in its middle, which the emperor Charles V is said to have regretted. Muslims are not allowed to pray there. See Spain.
